title: Acceptability of routine HIV counselling and testing, and HIV seroprevalence in Ugandan hospitals

sections.title: Page 1

summary.text: The opening page and abstract of a 2008 Bulletin study of routine HIV counselling and testing in Mulago and Mbarara hospitals, Uganda, where free routine testing began in November 2004. It outlines the objective, methods covering 25 wards and clinics through February 2006, the main findings on uptake and seroprevalence, and author and submission details.

sections.title: Page 2

summary.text: Describes the setting, history and structure of the routine HIV counselling and testing programme at the two Ugandan teaching hospitals, including earlier fee-based testing on request and a 2003 survey showing most inpatients had never been tested. It explains how the programme expanded across wards and clinics and how accessibility and uptake of testing were measured.

sections.extract: Rhoda K Wanyenze et al. Methods Setting Mulago and Mbarara hospitals are the largest, tertiary, public, university teach- ing hospitals in Uganda. Mulago hos- pital has more than 600 000 patient- visits per year while Mbarara hospital serves over 100 000 patients annually. sections.title: Page 3

summary.text: Presents the analysis approach and results of the Ugandan routine testing study: of 51 642 patients offered testing, 98% accepted, with lower uptake only at the STD clinic. It lists the reasons patients gave for declining and reports an overall HIV prevalence of 25% among those not previously known to be positive, most of whom had never been tested. It also notes higher risk among people unaware of their partners' HIV status.

sections.title: Page 4

summary.text: A table giving the number of patients tested, number HIV-positive and HIV prevalence by sex, age group, marital status, education and other characteristics in the Ugandan hospital testing study. Prevalence peaks among people in their thirties and among separated, divorced or widowed patients, and footnotes note an overall prevalence of 25% and some missing data.

sections.title: Page 5

summary.text: Discusses the Ugandan findings, including undetected discordance among couples, savings in time and transport, and limits on representativeness. It argues that expanding routine testing must be matched by more HIV care, health-worker training and possibly lay counsellors, and begins a table of adjusted odds ratios for HIV positivity among patients over 15.

sections.extract: Research Routine HIV testing in Ugandan hospitals Among couples who were tested, 100% of the HIV-negative members of discor- dant couples were previously unaware of their discordant status. These find- ings highlight the need to promote HIV testing for couples. Offering HCT to patients attending hospital saved them both time and transport expenses. sections.title: Page 6

summary.text: Concludes that routine HIV counselling and testing in Ugandan hospitals is feasible and should be part of scaled-up HIV services in high-prevalence settings, followed by acknowledgements, funding from the CDC and PEPFAR, and a competing-interests statement. The page then gives French and Spanish translations of the abstract.
